items.readable_text:
Content:
Every square matrix [MATH: A] can be written as

Content:
[MATH: A = PJP^{-1},]

Content:
where [MATH: J] is a Jordan canonical form and [MATH: P] is an invertible matrix.

Content:
Expressing [MATH: A] in the above form is called a Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A,] and is an extension of diagonalization that works for all square matrices.

Content:
So, to find a Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A] means to find both

Content:
- a Jordan canonical form [MATH: J,] and
- an invertible matrix [MATH: P] that satisfies the equation [MATH: A = PJP^{-1}].

Content:
If [MATH: A] is diagonalizable, finding a Jordan canonical decomposition is the same as diagonalizing. In this lesson, we will focus on non-diagonalizable matrices.

Content:
To find a Jordan canonical decomposition of a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix, we follow a three-step Jordan decomposition algorithm:

Content:
Step 1: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

Content:
We solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.] For the given matrix, there is only one eigenvalue, namely [MATH: \lambda = -2.]

Content:
Step 2: Find a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] consisting of the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to each eigenvalue.

Content:
Applying the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get an eigenvector

Content:
[MATH: [2; 1]]

Content:
corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = -2.] This is the first vector of our basis.

Content:
To find the second vector of our basis, we have to find a generalized eigenvector [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}] of [MATH: A] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = -2.] So, our vectors [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}] must form the following chain:

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}} \xrightarrow{A+2I} {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}} \xrightarrow{A+2I} \mathbf{0}]

Content:
Therefore, to find [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}] we must solve the equation

Content:
[MATH: (A +2I ){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} = {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}.]

Content:
Solving this equation using our usual methods gives us the solution

Content:
[MATH: [− 1; 0]]

Content:
Notice that the set [MATH: \left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}] is linearly independent and thus forms a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2.]

Content:
Step 3: Construct the matrices [MATH: J] and [MATH: P.]

Content:
Now that we have our special basis, we can construct a Jordan canonical form [MATH: J] and invertible matrix [MATH: P.]
The matrix [MATH: J] is represented by a single [MATH: 2 \times 2] Jordan block:

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|1; 0|− 2]]

Content:
Then, the columns of [MATH: P] are the vectors [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2,] where the first column must be the eigenvector [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}.] So, we get

Content:
[MATH: [|||; v_{1}|v_{2};|||]]

Content:
Finally, the Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A] is as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [− 4|4; − 1|0]]

Content:
Watch out! In Jordan decomposition, the order in which we write our vectors in the matrix [MATH: P] is important! The first column of [MATH: P] must always be the eigenvector.

[MATH: \lambda_1=\lambda_2=4.]

As a result, the first column of [MATH: P] corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda=4.]

Now, computing [MATH: A-4I,] we get

[MATH: A − 4I|= [8|4; − 4|0] − (4)[1|0; 0|1]; = [4|4; − 4|− 4].]

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix [MATH: M,] which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [4|4|0; − 4|− 4|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + R_{1}; ∼[4|4|0; 0|0|0]]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). Thus, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain [MATH: x_1=-x_2.] Hence, the general solution is

[MATH: [− x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Therefore, setting [MATH: x_2=1,] we get the eigenvector

[MATH: [a; b]]

Finally, [MATH: \dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-1}{1} = -1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Every square matrix [MATH: A] can be written as

Content:
[MATH: A = PJP^{-1},]

Content:
where [MATH: J] is a Jordan canonical form and [MATH: P] is an invertible matrix.

Content:
Expressing [MATH: A] in the above form is called a Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A,] and is an extension of diagonalization that works for all square matrices.

Content:
So, to find a Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A] means to find both

Content:
- a Jordan canonical form [MATH: J,] and
- an invertible matrix [MATH: P] that satisfies the equation [MATH: A = PJP^{-1}].

Content:
If [MATH: A] is diagonalizable, finding a Jordan canonical decomposition is the same as diagonalizing. In this lesson, we will focus on non-diagonalizable matrices.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: An Introductory Example

Content:
As an example, consider the following matrix:
[MATH: [0|1; − 4|4]]

Content:
This matrix has a single eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = {\color{red}2}] and, since [MATH: A] is not scalar, it is not diagonalizable. Thus, the Jordan canonical form of [MATH: A] is

Content:
[MATH: [2|1; 0|2]]

Content:
We can show that [MATH: A] has the Jordan canonical decomposition [MATH: A = PJP^{-1},] where

Content:
[MATH: [1|0; 2|1]]

Content:
Notice that the columns of [MATH: P] form a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] that generates the following chains:

Content:
[MATH: v_{2}→^(A − 2 I)v_{1}→^(A − 2 I)0]

Content:
The vectors [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}] and [MATH: {\color{DarkBlue}\mathbf{v}_2}] are generalized eigenvectors corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = {\color{red}2}.] Here, [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A,] while [MATH: {\color{DarkBlue}\mathbf{v}_2}] is a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 2.]

Content:
In general, the matrix [MATH: P] of any Jordan canonical decomposition of a non-diagonalizable [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: A] with eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] must satisfy the following property:

Content:
- The columns of [MATH: P] associated with a Jordan block [MATH: J_2(\lambda)] are generalized eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda,] where

- the first column of [MATH: P] is an eigenvector, and
- the second column of [MATH: P] is a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 2] that is mapped to the first column under the action of [MATH: A-\lambda I.]

Content:
Watch out! The order of the columns of [MATH: P] is important! The first column should always be an eigenvector.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Columns of a Transformation Matrix in a Jordan Decomposition

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [3|− 4; 1|− 1]]

Consider the matrices above. Given that [MATH: A = P J P^{-1}] is a Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A,] which of the following could be the second column of the matrix [MATH: P?]

[MATH: [1; 0]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix [MATH: J] consists of one Jordan block [MATH: J = J_2(1).]

Therefore, the columns of [MATH: P] form the following chain:

[MATH: J_{2}(1)|:|v_{2}→^(A − 1 I)v_{1}→^(A − 1 I)0]

As a result, the second column of [MATH: P] is a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 2] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda=1.]

Now, computing [MATH: A-1I,] we get

[MATH: A − 1I|= [3|− 4; 1|− 1] − 1[1|0; 0|1] = [2|− 4; 1|− 2].]

Among the given vectors, only [MATH: \mathbf x] is a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 2,] since

[MATH: [2|− 4; 1|− 2]]
and
[MATH: [2|− 4; 1|− 2]]

Therefore, we can write

[MATH: [1; 0]→^(A − 1 I)[2; 1]→^(A − 1 I)0.]

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

Item 6 — Tutorial: Finding the Jordan Decomposition of a Non-Diagonalizable 2x2 Matrix

Content:
Let's find the Jordan canonical decomposition of the matrix [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [− 4|4; − 1|0]]

Content:
To find a Jordan canonical decomposition of a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix, we follow a three-step Jordan decomposition algorithm:

Content:
Step 1: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

Content:
We solve the characteristic equation [MATH: \vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.] For the given matrix, there is only one eigenvalue, namely [MATH: \lambda = -2.]

Content:
Step 2: Find a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] consisting of the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to each eigenvalue.

Content:
Applying the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get an eigenvector

Content:
[MATH: [2; 1]]

Content:
corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = -2.] This is the first vector of our basis.

Content:
To find the second vector of our basis, we have to find a generalized eigenvector [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}] of [MATH: A] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = -2.] So, our vectors [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}] must form the following chain:

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}} \xrightarrow{A+2I} {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}} \xrightarrow{A+2I} \mathbf{0}]

Content:
Therefore, to find [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}] we must solve the equation

Content:
[MATH: (A +2I ){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} = {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}.]

Content:
Solving this equation using our usual methods gives us the solution

Content:
[MATH: [− 1; 0]]

Content:
Notice that the set [MATH: \left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}] is linearly independent and thus forms a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2.]

Content:
Step 3: Construct the matrices [MATH: J] and [MATH: P.]

Content:
Now that we have our special basis, we can construct a Jordan canonical form [MATH: J] and invertible matrix [MATH: P.]
The matrix [MATH: J] is represented by a single [MATH: 2 \times 2] Jordan block:

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|1; 0|− 2]]

Content:
Then, the columns of [MATH: P] are the vectors [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2,] where the first column must be the eigenvector [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}.] So, we get

Content:
[MATH: [|||; v_{1}|v_{2};|||]]

Content:
Finally, the Jordan canonical decomposition of [MATH: A] is as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [− 4|4; − 1|0]]

Content:
Watch out! In Jordan decomposition, the order in which we write our vectors in the matrix [MATH: P] is important! The first column of [MATH: P] must always be the eigenvector.

---
